title: Common eigenvector for a finite commuting family over an algebraically closed field
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field], [def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], let $I$ be a finite set (possibly empty), and let $T_i:V\to V$ be $k$-linear endomorphisms indexed by $i\in I$. Assume $T_iT_j=T_jT_i$ for every $i,j\in I$, where products denote composition. There exist $v\in V\setminus\{0\}$ and scalars $\lambda_i\in k$ for all $i\in I$ such that $T_i(v)=\lambda_i v$ for every $i\in I$.

source.place: Lemma 16.11, printed p.327, proof: the induction proving existence of a one-dimensional stable subspace; finite-family consequence.

proof.text: Induct on $n=|I|$, with the assertion quantified over every nonzero finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and every commuting family indexed by an $n$-element set. For $n=0$, choose $v\ne0$ using $V\ne0$; the unique empty family of scalars has the required vacuous property. For the induction step take $n>0$, fix $i_0\in I$, and put $J=I\setminus\{i_0\}$, so $|J|=n-1$. The induction hypothesis is available for families on any nonzero finite-dimensional space, not just on $V$.

source.place: Lemma 16.11, printed p.327, proof: restriction to an invariant eigenspace. The finite-family version here uses induction on the number of operators instead of dimension.

proof.text: Apply [lem-zl-alg-closed-endomorphism-eigenvalue] to $T_{i_0}$ on $V$: choose $a\in k$ and $z\ne0$ with $T_{i_0}(z)=az$. Put $E=\{x\in V:T_{i_0}(x)=ax\}$. Linearity shows that $0\in E$, and that $T_{i_0}(bx+cy)=a(bx+cy)$ for $x,y\in E$ and $b,c\in k$, so $E$ is a $k$-linear subspace. It is nonzero because $z\in E$. Apply [lem-trf-vector-space-quotient-dimension] with $U=E$ to conclude that $E$ is finite-dimensional; only its subspace-finiteness clause is used. Thus $E$ satisfies every vector-space hypothesis of the induction assertion.

source.place: Lemma 16.11, printed p.327, proof: restriction to an invariant eigenspace. The finite-family version here uses induction on the number of operators instead of dimension.

proof.text: For $j\in J$ and $x\in E$, compute $T_{i_0}(T_jx)=T_j(T_{i_0}x)=T_j(ax)=aT_jx$ by commutativity and linearity. Hence $T_j(E)\subseteq E$ and $S_j=T_j|_E:E\to E$ is linear. For $j,l\in J$ the two composites on $x\in E$ have ambient values $T_j(T_lx)=T_l(T_jx)$, so the restricted operators commute. Apply the induction hypothesis to $(S_j)_{j\in J}$ on the nonzero finite-dimensional space $E$: obtain $v\in E\setminus\{0\}$ and $b_j\in k$ with $S_j(v)=b_jv$. The inclusion $E\subseteq V$ is injective, so this same $v$ is nonzero in $V$. Set $\lambda_{i_0}=a$ and $\lambda_j=b_j$ for $j\in J$. Membership $v\in E$ gives $T_{i_0}(v)=av$, and the equations for the restrictions give $T_j(v)=b_jv$ for every $j\in J$. This proves the induction step and all the required equations.
